corrections.source_says: Set n_units to 214 concepts: the paper explicitly reports 214 concepts in total, and Table 9 reports 107 concepts in each condition. These are outputs from the same 35 analyzed students. Retain the existing note that the stated total is inconsistent with six concepts per student; do not replace the printed total with a calculated count.
corrections.quote: To assess artifact-level creativity, we collected 214 concepts (six per participant in the full sample) across the six briefs.
corrections.locator: PDF p. 13, Section 4.3.3; p. 17, Section 4.5.1; p. 21, Table 9 (idea-level rows)

corrections.source_says: Populate this field with the complete-case inclusion and attrition information already partly recorded in participants.who: 96 students were enrolled, 63 consented, and 35 submitted all required questionnaires, concept templates and ChatGPT transcripts and entered the final sample. The paper reports attrition of 44.5%. One invalid birth-year response was excluded only from age analysis; that student remained in the other analyses. These are completion counts, not randomized counts.
corrections.quote: Attrition (44.5%) may have occurred because participation in the research components (questionnaires and transcripts) was entirely voluntary within a mandatory course activity.
corrections.locator: PDF p. 9, Section 4.1, recruitment/completion and demographics paragraphs

corrections.form_value: Among 35 design students who ideated first without AI and then with ChatGPT (fixed order), expert-rated creativity did not differ between conditions (participant level 3.37 vs 3.29, Z = -0.418, p = .676; idea level 3.25 vs 3.37, Z = -0.281, p = .779; pp. 21-22, Tables 9-10), while self-reported confidence, engagement, stimulation, flow, and energy were lower with ChatGPT.
corrections.source_says: The numbers are correct, but label 3.37 versus 3.29 and 3.25 versus 3.37 as medians from Table 9, and replace "did not differ" with "no statistically significant difference was detected". The participant-level outcome is each student’s mean score across concepts, whose between-student median is reported in Table 9; the table does not report arm means. Retain Z = -0.418, p = .676 at participant level and Z = -0.281, p = .779 at idea level. The lower self-reported confidence and experience claims are supported, but add their locators: pp. 18-21, Sections 5.2.1-5.2.2, Tables 2 and 8.
corrections.quote: Similarly, the test comparing participants’ mean creativity scores showed no significant difference between the two conditions, z = −0.418, p = .676 (see Table 10).
corrections.locator: PDF p. 15, Section 4.3.3; p. 17, Section 4.5.1 (non-significant findings); pp. 18-21, Sections 5.2.1-5.2.2 and Tables 2, 8; pp. 21-22, Tables 9-10 and Section 5.2.3

confirmed: Read the entire on-file markdown, including the closing material and references (PDF pp. 1-38); checked every number quoted in the form against the relevant PDF pages, and visually checked Table 10 where text extraction corrupted minus signs.

The source is the 38-page Design Science journal version of record, vol. 12, e16 (2026): received 15 April 2025, revised 22 April 2026, accepted 23 April 2026, downloaded 5 October 2026. The title and five authors match the form (PDF p. 1).

No randomized people study is reported. Everyone completed no-GenAI ideation first and ChatGPT ideation second; the authors explicitly describe the study as non-randomized (PDF p. 10, Section 4.2; p. 32, Section 6.5). The quasi_people design and observational context classification are correct under the codebook and form-spec.

The final analyzed sample is 35 students, the same people in both conditions, drawn from 63 consenting students among 96 enrolled; randomized counts appropriately remain null. Ages 20–29 and 77.1% female match the source (PDF p. 9, Section 4.1). The sample is below 50, so core eligibility fails both randomization and sample-size criteria.

The assignment involved second-year UX Design students, six shared-space briefs, three concepts per condition, ChatGPT 3.5 via the free web model, and two weeks of individual homework (PDF pp. 8-11, Sections 4-4.3.1).

Expert ratings satisfy the scored-output criterion: two designers rated concepts blind to condition; dimensions used in analysis were originality, applicability, effectiveness and clarity, on 5-point scales, with Workability removed. Participant scores averaged three concepts per condition (PDF pp. 13 and 15, Section 4.3.3).

Both reported strings correctly reproduce Table 9. Participant-level rows: Without GenAI N = 35, median 3.37, SD .537, min 2.16, max 4.42; With ChatGPT N = 35, median 3.29, SD .574, min 1.42, max 4.04 (PDF p. 21, Table 9).

Idea-level rows: Without GenAI N = 107 concepts, median 3.25, SD .706, min 1.25, max 4.75; With ChatGPT N = 107 concepts, median 3.37, SD .824, min 1.13, max 4.88. The form correctly flags the unexplained inconsistency between 214 concepts and six per student (PDF p. 13, Section 4.3.3; p. 21, Table 9).

Participant-level test: Z = -0.418, r-signed = -0.07, 95% CI [-0.39; 0.27], p-raw 0.676, p-Holm 1.352. The value 1.352 really is printed and should not be silently repaired (PDF p. 22, Table 10 and Section 5.2.3).

Idea-level test: Z = -0.281, r-signed = -0.03, 95% CI [-0.22; 0.17], p-raw 0.779, p-Holm 0.779; prose prints z = -.281, p = .779. These are paired Wilcoxon tests, with Rosenthal’s r and Fisher-z confidence intervals, not standardized mean differences (PDF pp. 16-17, Section 4.5.1; p. 22, Table 10 and Section 5.2.3).

Lower self-reported confidence, engagement, stimulation, flow and energy are supported by the reported tests, including Holm-adjusted significance; these are self-reports rather than additional scored-output creativity outcomes (PDF pp. 18-21, Sections 5.2.1-5.2.2 and Tables 2, 8).

The three-student first-year pilot refined the concept template; the five follow-up interviewees were a subset of the main sample. Neither is reported as a separate randomized AI-assistance study with scored creative outputs (PDF pp. 10-11, Sections 4.2 and 4.3.1).

The external supplementary material is described as containing the concept template (Appendix A) and interview script; it is not included in the main PDF and was not independently read in this check. The form’s supplement description is supported by the main article (PDF p. 11, Section 4.3.1; p. 15, Section 4.3.4; p. 33, Supplementary material).
This is an original empirical study, not a synthesis; leaving pooled estimates empty is appropriate (PDF pp. 8-17, Methods; pp. 18-25, Results).
summary: The fixed-order, non-randomized study analyzed 35 students and is correctly classified as quasi_people with observational context. The reported table values are accurate; three corrections address the missing concept count and attrition field, and clarify the one-line finding’s median labels and non-significant result.
